structure.title: Chapters 1–27 · A bed, a friend and a ship
structure.text: Ishmael goes to sea when life ashore begins to sour. Before he has seen a whale, he must share a bed with a stranger and bargain over wages. Queequeg proves easier to trust than the pious owners who mean to pay them both a fraction of the catch.

structure.title: Chapters 28–47 · Ahab names his object
structure.text: The captain appears late and gathers the crew round a coin nailed to the mast. Hunting whales for oil and hunting one whale for vengeance now have to occupy the same ship. Only one of those enterprises was in the agreement the sailors signed.

structure.title: Chapters 48–99 · The work between sightings
structure.text: Chapters on skin, blubber, rope and the division of a carcass interrupt the pursuit. They supply what obsession leaves out. A single animal is a living body to a naturalist, a fortune to the owners and a set of immediate dangers to the people leaning over the gunwale.

structure.title: Chapter 100 – epilogue · Other ships and the chase
structure.text: Encounters with other captains bring partial news of the white whale and competing reasons for turning back. By the time the search narrows to consecutive days of pursuit, the reader has seen how many kinds of work, knowledge and allegiance Ahab must bend to one purpose.

people.name: Ishmael
people.text: He can describe squeezing whale oil among shipmates with something like religious ecstasy, then sound like a librarian quarrelling over how to shelve a whale. His pleasure in pursuing another comparison makes him a curious witness to a captain who recognises only one.

people.name: Queequeg
people.text: The man who terrifies Ishmael at the inn turns out to be a considerate bedfellow. On the ship his skill keeps people alive who would have been quite prepared to dismiss him on shore.

people.name: Ahab and Starbuck
people.text: Ahab reads the injury done to his body as something he can answer by striking back. Starbuck has signed on to make money for the owners and return to his family. To oppose his captain he would have to break the obedience that makes his profession possible.

context.title: A wage tied to the catch
context.text: A sailor's lay is his share of the proceeds. The owners' negotiations matter later when the captain proposes his private expedition. Everybody on deck has already invested labour and future pay in a voyage whose purpose one man can change.

context.title: What happens to a whale alongside the ship
context.text: The crew strip long spirals of blubber from the carcass, cut it into smaller pieces and render it in furnaces aboard the ship. At night the work lights the deck from below. One animal can turn a sailing vessel into a floating factory before the hunt resumes.

notice.text: Follow a rope from one body to another.
notice.why: Harpoon lines can drag a sailor out of a boat. A line tied between two men can make one man's footing depend on the other's. Ishmael's meditations on human fellowship repeatedly begin with an arrangement of actual rope.

passages.quote: the monkey-rope was fast at both ends

notice.text: Listen to the men looking at the gold coin.
notice.why: The object stays nailed in place while each observer discovers a private message in its design. In a few pages the mast becomes a small version of the ocean on which they all profess to see the same whale.

opening: Ishmael goes to sea because life ashore is making him dangerous company. A whaling voyage promises work, distance, and strangers worth meeting. Then his captain reveals a purpose the crew did not sign up for: Ahab wants the white whale that took his leg. Melville makes room for friendship, filthy jokes, sermons, and astonishing quantities of whale knowledge while a private obsession gathers command of a ship. The men have their own reasons for sailing; their captain intends to give them his.
